definition: Disenfranchisement means the state of being deprived of a legal right, especially the right to vote.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word disenfranchisement. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know disenfranchisement should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: In the 1890s, poll taxes across the American South achieved the deliberate disenfranchisement of Black voters, who could not cast a ballot without paying a fee many could never afford.

Marginalization is the gradual pushing of a group to society's edges in many ways at once — ignored in media, passed over for jobs, unheard in politics. Disenfranchisement is one specific, formal blow: the removal of a legal right, above all the vote. Marginalization is diffuse; disenfranchisement is on the books.

Exclusion is any shutting-out, formal or casual — from a meeting, a team, a conversation. Disenfranchisement is exclusion of one precise kind: carried out by stripping away a legal right, especially the right to vote. Every disenfranchisement excludes, but most exclusions take away no legal right at all.

Disempowerment is a general draining of power, confidence, or influence, by any means. Disenfranchisement is narrower and more official: the loss of a legally recognized right, above all the vote. A community can feel disempowered by neglect alone; disenfranchisement requires that some right actually be taken away.
Inclusion brings people into full participation rather than barring them from it.
Empowerment builds up a person's power and standing instead of stripping it away.

In 1911 the port city of Halvern rewrote its charter: from that year on, only property owners could vote in city elections.
Renters — dockworkers, seamstresses, clerks — made up two-thirds of the population, and every one of them lost the ballot overnight.
Nothing else about their lives changed on paper; they kept their jobs, their unions, their churches, and their newspapers.
But councilmen no longer answered their letters, and paving crews stopped coming to their streets, because their disenfranchisement had made them safe to ignore.
It took a nineteen-year campaign to strike the property clause, and the first thing the restored voters did was unseat every councilman who had supported it.
